Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

# Conservative Party Manifesto 1997: Summary

## Core Vision and Economic Record

The 1997 Conservative manifesto presented a stark choice between continuing Conservative economic success and risking it all with Labour's alternative approach. The party positioned itself as having transformed Britain from "the sick man of Europe" into its most successful economy since 1979.

The manifesto highlighted key achievements: inflation below 4% for over four years, unemployment lower than any major European economy, and Britain attracting one-third of all EU inward investment. The Conservatives championed their low-tax philosophy, with public spending around 40% of national income compared to 50% on the continent.

## Economic Strategy

The Conservatives pledged to continue tight control of public spending while reducing the basic income tax rate to 20p. They committed to maintaining inflation at 2.5% or less and opposed the "European social model" of regulation, explicitly refusing to sign the Social Chapter or introduce a national minimum wage.

The manifesto emphasised support for small businesses through corporation tax cuts, business rate reform, and regulatory reduction. It championed free markets and warned that Labour's "stakeholding" approach would burden businesses and destroy jobs.

## Family and Welfare

Central to Conservative ideology was transferring power from the state to families. Proposals included allowing non-working spouses to transfer their tax allowance to their partner, worth up to £17.50 weekly. A revolutionary pension reform would provide young workers with personal pension funds through national insurance rebates, eventually replacing state dependency with private ownership.

## Public Services

Rather than expanding state provision, the Conservatives advocated market-based reforms. The NHS would receive increased funding but through private finance initiatives. Schools would gain independence from local authorities, with more grammar schools and specialist schools expanding parental choice. The party opposed "progressive education" and championed traditional teaching methods and rigorous testing.

## Law and Order

The manifesto took a hardline position on crime, proposing mandatory minimum sentences for persistent offenders, expanded CCTV surveillance, and measures targeting juvenile crime including Parental Control Orders. It emphasised that "prison works" and pledged 8,500 additional prison places.

## Constitution and Europe

The Conservatives presented themselves as defenders of the Union against devolution, which they argued would "pull apart" the United Kingdom. On Europe, they sought "a partnership of nation states" rather than federalism, maintaining Britain's veto and opt-out from the Social Chapter. While keeping options open on the single currency, they guaranteed a referendum before any decision to join.

## Conclusion

The manifesto articulated a coherent conservative vision: minimal state intervention, low taxation, individual responsibility, traditional values, strong national sovereignty, and scepticism toward European integration—positioning these as proven successes against what it portrayed as Labour's dangerous statism.

# Summary of the 1997 Labour Party Manifesto: "New Labour Because Britain Deserves Better"

## Vision and Philosophy

The manifesto presents Tony Blair's "New Labour" as a transformative political project transcending traditional left-right divisions. The core philosophy is explicitly pragmatic: "What counts is what works. The objectives are radical. The means will be modern." This represents a deliberate break from Labour's past, having rewritten the party's constitution to embrace enterprise alongside justice.

New Labour positions itself as a broad national movement representing "the British people as a whole" rather than sectional interests. The vision is "national renewal"—a confident, unified Britain equipped for the global economy with modernised public services and accountable politics.

## Economic Framework

The manifesto commits to fiscal prudence and economic stability as prerequisites for growth. Key pledges include no increases to basic or top income tax rates, adherence to existing spending limits for two years, strict borrowing rules, and a long-term goal of a ten-pence starting tax rate. The approach is explicitly "save to invest, not tax and spend."

Economic policy accepts globalisation as reality while promoting competitiveness through skills, infrastructure investment, and public-private partnerships. A reformed competition law, reinvigorated Private Finance Initiative, and support for small businesses form the business agenda. A national minimum wage, set sensibly through an independent commission, would tackle low pay while maintaining flexibility.

## Welfare-to-Work

A centrepiece "welfare-to-work" programme, funded by a windfall levy on privatised utilities, would provide 250,000 young unemployed with options: subsidised private-sector jobs, voluntary sector work, education, or environmental taskforce positions. Crucially, remaining on full benefit would not be permitted—"rights and duties go together."

## Public Services

Education is declared "number one priority," with commitments to cut infant class sizes to 30, guarantee nursery places, modernise comprehensives through setting by ability, and attack underperformance through intervention and "Education Action Zones."

NHS reform promises to end the Conservative internal market while retaining separation between planning and provision. The first £100 million saved from bureaucracy would treat 100,000 additional patients. A public health minister would address root causes of illness, including banning tobacco advertising.

## Law and Order

The manifesto emphasises being "tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime." Proposals include halving processing time for young offenders, decentralising the Crown Prosecution Service, community safety orders, and zero tolerance of disorder. A free vote would be permitted on banning handguns.

## Constitutional Reform

Extensive democratic renewal is promised: devolution to Scotland and Wales following referendums, ending hereditary peers' voting rights, an elected London mayor and assembly, regional development agencies, freedom of information legislation, and incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.

## Europe and Foreign Policy

Labour commits to leadership in Europe—signing the Social Chapter, pursuing single market completion, CAP reform, and EU enlargement—while opposing a federal superstate. A referendum would precede any single currency decision. Defence policy retains Trident while pursuing multilateral disarmament and UN reform, with renewed emphasis on combating global poverty.

The manifesto concludes with five specific pledges as Labour's "contract with the people"—a covenant designed to rebuild trust in government through achievable, measurable commitments.
